LANDLORD'S RIGHT OF ENTRY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Properties, LLC · Jordan T. Reyes

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California statutory law on when and how Acme Properties, LLC, as landlord, may enter the residential dwelling unit rented by Jordan T. Reyes at 456 Maple Street, Apt 2, Oakland, CA. It states what California law provides on this subject. It does not authorize, direct, or prohibit any particular entry, and it does not tell either Acme Properties, LLC or Jordan T. Reyes what to do about any specific situation.

PERMITTED PURPOSES FOR ENTRY
California law allows a landlord to enter a tenant's dwelling unit only in specific listed cases: (1) in case of emergency; (2) to make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations, or improvements, to supply necessary or agreed services, or to exhibit the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, mortgagee, tenant, worker, or contractor, or to make a security-deposit pre-move-out inspection; (3) when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit; or (4) under a court order. Two further categories of permitted entry are cross-referenced within this same statute but defined elsewhere: one for purposes set out in a separate chapter of the Civil Code beginning at section 1954.201, and one for compliance with a specific article of the Health and Safety Code beginning at section 17973 — neither of which this information sheet covers. Beyond these listed purposes, a landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "A landlord may enter the dwelling unit only in the following cases: (1) In case of emergency. (2) To make necessary or agreed repairs, decorations, alterations or improvements, supply necessary or agreed services, or exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, mortgagees, tenants, workers, or contractors or to make an inspection pursuant to subdivision (f) of Section 1950.5. (3) When the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises. (4) Pursuant to court order."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a)(1)-(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the four general permitted purposes for entry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "(5) For the purposes set forth in Chapter 2.5 (commencing with Section 1954.201). (6) To comply with the provisions of Article 2.2 (commencing with Section 17973) of Chapter 5 of Part 1.5 of Division 13 of the Health and Safety Code."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(a)(5)-(6) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the two cross-referenced additional categories this document doesn't cover (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "The landlord may not abuse the right of access or use it to harass the tenant."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, no abuse or harassment (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of what California law provides on landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; the permitted purposes for landlord entry, and what counts as their abuse, vary by state. All three citations below are subsections of the same statutory section (§ 1954) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for the enumerated-purposes list itself. Separately: this document's author attempted to research published California case law construing what conduct counts as "abuse" of the right of access under subdivision (c), using a case-law search tool, but that tool's research-request limit was exhausted before a citable result could be verified against the tool's own text — rather than state or invent a case citation on that point, this information sheet omits one. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry was or would be lawful.

WRITTEN NOTICE: CONTENT, DELIVERY, AND THE REASONABLE-NOTICE PRESUMPTIONS
Except for the narrower situations addressed elsewhere in this information sheet, California law requires a landlord to give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of the landlord's intent to enter, and to enter only during normal business hours. The written notice must include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. It may be delivered by personal delivery to the tenant, by leaving it with someone of suitable age and discretion at the premises, by leaving it on, near, or under the usual entry door in a manner a reasonable person would discover it, or by mailing it to the tenant. California law sets two separate rebuttable presumptions of what counts as reasonable notice: twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice generally, and — separately — mailing the notice at least six days before the intended entry is presumed reasonable notice for a mailed notice specifically. Both are rebuttable presumptions, not fixed floors; either can be shown to be unreasonable, or reasonable, by evidence in a particular case.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except as provided in subdivision (e), or as provided in paragraph (2) or (3), the landlord shall give the tenant reasonable notice in writing of his or her intent to enter and enter only during normal business hours. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. The notice may be personally delivered to the tenant, left with someone of a suitable age and discretion at the premises, or, left on, near, or under the usual entry door of the premises in a manner in which a reasonable person would discover the notice."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, written notice content and delivery methods (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "Twenty-four hours shall be presumed to be reasonable notice in absence of evidence to the contrary. The notice may be mailed to the tenant. Mailing of the notice at least six days prior to an intended entry is presumed reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the 24-hour and six-day-mailing presumptions (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's notice requirement for landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; the length and form of required notice, and whether a state even sets a numeric presumption at all, vary by state. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection (§ 1954(d)(1)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific notice given, or entry made, was or would be reasonable.

NORMAL BUSINESS HOURS
Except in an emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit, California law bars entry outside normal business hours unless the tenant consents, at the time of entry, to an entry outside normal business hours.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "Except in cases of emergency or when the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the premises, entry may not be made during other than normal business hours unless the tenant consents to an entry during other than normal business hours at the time of entry."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, entry limited to normal business hours (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: The statute restricts entry to "normal business hours" but does not itself define that phrase with a specific clock-time range; this information sheet states the restriction as written and doesn't supply a numeric definition the statute doesn't provide. This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's time-of-day restriction on landlord entry — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; not every state restricts entry by time of day, and the ones that do vary in how they phrase the restriction. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry was or would be within normal business hours.

WHEN NO NOTICE AT ALL IS REQUIRED
In three specific situations, California law requires no notice of entry at all: to respond to an emergency; if the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry; and after the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "No notice of entry is required under this section: (1) To respond to an emergency. (2) If the tenant is present and consents to the entry at the time of entry. (3) After the tenant has abandoned or surrendered the unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(e) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, when no notice at all is required (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of when California law dispenses with notice altogether — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; which circumstances excuse notice, and whether a state excuses notice at all, vary by state. This is a single statutory subsection; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether a specific tenant's presence, consent, or abandonment of the unit actually excused notice in any given instance.

TWO NARROWER EXCEPTIONS TO WRITTEN NOTICE: SHOWING THE PROPERTY TO A BUYER, AND AGREED REPAIR VISITS
California law creates two narrower exceptions to the ordinary written-notice requirement, each tied to a specific circumstance. First, if the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser — by its own terms, this exception covers purchasers, not prospective tenants — the landlord may give oral notice, in person or by telephone, but only if the landlord or the landlord's agent has already given the tenant separate written notice, within the preceding 120 days, that the property is for sale and that oral contact for this purpose may follow. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice for this oral notice as well, and the notice must still include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry; at the time of entry, the landlord or agent must leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit. Second, the tenant and landlord may agree orally to an entry for agreed repairs or agreed services, with no written notice at all, if the oral agreement itself includes the date and approximate time of entry and the entry occurs within one week of the agreement.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "If the purpose of the entry is to exhibit the dwelling unit to prospective or actual purchasers, the notice may be given orally, in person or by telephone, if the landlord or his or her agent has notified the tenant in writing within 120 days of the oral notice that the property is for sale and that the landlord or agent may contact the tenant orally for the purpose described above. Twenty-four hours is presumed reasonable notice in the absence of evidence to the contrary. The notice shall include the date, approximate time, and purpose of the entry. At the time of entry, the landlord or agent shall leave written evidence of the entry inside the unit."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(2) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, oral notice to show the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  "The tenant and the landlord may agree orally to an entry to make agreed repairs or supply agreed services. The agreement shall include the date and approximate time of the entry, which shall be within one week of the agreement. In this case, the landlord is not required to provide the tenant a written notice."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1954(d)(3) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, an oral agreement for a repair or service visit needs no written notice (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1954.)
  Known gap: This is one state's statute, used as evidence of California's specific reduced-notice exceptions — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; some states relax the notice requirement for showing a unit to a new prospective tenant near the end of a tenancy, but California's statute, on its face, does not: its oral-notice exception in this section is written to cover showing the unit to a prospective or actual purchaser, not to a prospective new tenant, and California's statute sets no separate "48 hours' oral notice" figure for either circumstance — that specific figure, to the extent it describes a real rule, describes a different state's law, not California's. Both citations below are drawn from the same statutory subsection (§ 1954(d)) rather than independently authored sources; no additional independent source was found for this. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific oral notice given, or oral agreement reached, satisfied this section.

WHAT HAPPENS IF A LANDLORD VIOLATES THIS SECTION
Civil Code section 1954 does not itself set out a penalty or remedy for its own violation. A separate statute makes it unlawful for a landlord to do certain things for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling, and one of the listed things is committing a significant and intentional violation of section 1954; a tenant who prevails in a civil action — including in small claims court — to enforce rights under that separate statute is entitled to a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. Apart from that specific statute, California law separately provides that an agreement to let real property binds the landlord to secure the tenant's quiet possession of the premises against all persons lawfully claiming it; a landlord's interference with a tenant's use of the unit can also be evaluated under that separate covenant, which is a different body of law from section 1954 itself.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-02]
  "It is unlawful for a landlord to do any of the following for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the purpose requirement for this separate unlawful-conduct statute (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "Commit a significant and intentional violation of Section 1954."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a)(4) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, a significant and intentional violation of section 1954 as unlawful conduct (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including an action in small claims court, to enforce his or her rights under this section is entitled to a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed two thousand dollars ($2,000) for each violation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(b) (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the civil penalty for a prevailing tenant (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "An agreement to let upon hire binds the letter to secure to the hirer the quiet possession of the thing hired during the term of the hiring, against all persons lawfully claiming the same."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1927 (California Legislative Information text), California Civil Code, the separate covenant of quiet possession (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1927.)
  Known gap: These are one state's statutes, used together as evidence of what happens under California law when a landlord violates the entry statute — not a claim about which state's law governs any particular reader's tenancy; whether an entry-notice statute carries its own penalty, and what that penalty is, vary by state. Three of the four citations below (the two from § 1940.2(a) and the one from § 1940.2(b)) are subsections of the same statutory section rather than independently authored sources; the fourth citation, § 1927, is a separate, independently enacted statutory section (in force since 1872) supplying a different legal basis — the quiet-possession covenant — so it is treated here as a genuinely separate source, not additional corroboration of § 1940.2. Note also that the § 1940.2 penalty is narrower than a bare violation of § 1954: it requires the violation to be both significant and intentional, and committed for the purpose of influencing the tenant to vacate — an ordinary, isolated, or unintentional violation of § 1954 does not, by this statute's own terms, trigger this specific penalty. This document's author also attempted to locate citable published California case law applying either statute to a landlord's entry practices, using a case-law search tool, but that tool's research-request limit was exhausted before a citable result could be verified against the tool's own text; rather than state or invent a case citation, this information sheet relies on the statutory text alone. This document is informational only; it does not itself authorize or prohibit any specific entry, and it does not determine whether any specific entry violated either statute or gives rise to any remedy.

This information sheet regarding entry to the rental unit at 456 Maple Street, Apt 2, Oakland, CA, leased by Acme Properties, LLC to Jordan T. Reyes, states California law as of the date below. It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any particular entry.
